insights: Observation: activity.csv has 10,299 rows and 563 columns; the profiled columns show no missing values, activity has 6 unique labels, and subject has 30 unique IDs.
Observation: the context names five activities, but the profile reports six unique activity values; the label set should be verified before interpreting sitting/standing confusion.
Observation: 561 columns are engineered sensor features, including many time-domain and frequency-domain variants of the same axes, so high redundancy and correlated features are expected.

Observation: subject is an identifier for people, not a sensor feature, and should be excluded from model inputs to avoid person-level leakage.
Observation: no timestamp column is present in the supplied schema, so temporal leakage cannot be assessed directly; subject grouping is the available leakage control.
Hypothesis: a group-disjoint split by subject will better estimate performance for unseen people than random row splitting, because sensor distributions may vary by person.
Hypothesis: tree ensembles should be competitive on this wide tabular sensor table, but high dimensionality and only 30 subject groups may make validation estimates noisy.

config.preparation: No joins or derived columns. Use activity.csv as a single table. Target is activity. Exclude subject from features because it is the group identifier for unseen-person evaluation; exclude activity as the target. Retain all 561 sensor features using features=['*'] with no additional feature exclusions initially. Use a reproducible group holdout split on subject so all rows for a subject are in only one of train/validation/final. Use standard preprocessing (median imputation, bounded one-hot encoding, scaling) as the initial baseline. No label-end column or forward-looking fields are present.
config.rationale: The objective is to classify activity for unseen people, so a group split by subject is required to avoid person-level leakage. Macro F1 is appropriate for multi-class activity recognition and highlights sitting/standing errors. Standard preprocessing is a safe initial baseline; tree ensembles (Random Forest, LightGBM, XGBoost) are CPU-friendly and robust to correlated high-dimensional sensor features. No augmentations are used initially because class counts are unknown and group-disjoint splits can make minority classes small. This setup does not claim comparability with the original published train/test split or raw-signal preprocessing.
